kernelIdea: "If p then q" claims only that q holds whenever p does. It is false only when p is true and q is false, so it is automatically true when p is false — this is vacuous truth.

kernels.l1: A promise about rain is broken in only one way: it rains and you don't have the umbrella.
kernels.l2: An if-then promise is broken in one bad case: the if-part is true but the then-part isn't. Every other day the promise stays kept.
kernels.l3: An if-then claim promises that whenever the 'if' part holds, the 'then' part holds too. It is false only when the 'if' part is true and the 'then' part is false.
kernels.l4: A conditional 'if p then q' is false only when p is true and q is false. When p is false, the conditional is automatically true — this is vacuous truth.
kernels.l5: A conditional is false in exactly one case: hypothesis true, conclusion false. When the hypothesis fails, the conditional is vacuously true.
kernels.l6: A conditional is false only in the row where the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. Every other row — including both with the hypothesis false — makes it vacuously true.
kernels.l7: A conditional is false only when the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails; the two rows with a false hypothesis make it vacuously true. So proving one reduces to ruling out that single row.
kernels.l8: The material conditional p ⇒ q is defined to be false only when p is true and q is false; every other case, including both in which p is false, makes it (vacuously) true, which is what makes universally quantified statements over empty domains automatically true.
